items.title: UK GDPR, Article 24: Responsibility of the controller
items.quote: the measures referred to in paragraph 1 shall include the implementation of appropriate data protection policies by the controller
items.why: The nearest thing to a statutory policy duty. Where proportionate, a controller's compliance measures must include data protection policies. It covers personal data only, and does not mention AI or acceptable use.

items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.locator: Principle A, p.6; Principle I, p.8
items.quote: The board should ensure that the necessary resources, policies and practices are in place for the company to meet its objectives
items.why: The board-level hook for a policy set in listed companies. Principle I adds that the board should ensure it has the policies and processes it needs to function. Comply or explain; the Code does not mention AI or say which policies are needed.

items.title: Annual Review of Corporate Governance Reporting
items.locator: p.45 (AI policy and reporting; closing paragraph of the AI section); sample on p.5
items.quote: It is important that there are clear policies and procedures that are embedded across all levels of the organisation.
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation and figure. Of a sample of 100 companies, 'Eleven companies reported having an AI policy or reviewing their code of conduct to include a section on AI'. This is the regulator's view in a review of reporting, not a Code provision. It does not set an expectation for a named reporting season, as the existing briefing claims.

items.title: Supervisory Statement SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Principle 2.3 (Policies and procedures), points (a)-(c), PDF p.15-16
items.quote: Firm-wide policies should be approved by the board and reviewed on a regular basis
items.why: The most specific UK regulatory text on approval and currency: board approval, regular review for continued relevance to the regulatory landscape and to 'new and advancing technologies', and compliance reported to the board. Applies only to banks, building societies and designated investment firms with internal model approval.

items.title: AI Management Essentials tool (consultation version, accessible)
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: We have a clear, accessible and suitable AI policy for our organisation.
items.why: Government's own checklist of what an AI policy should do: exist, be available to all employees, help users judge whether a use is appropriate, identify roles and responsibilities, and be reviewed on a stated cycle. This is the consultation version; the consultation closed on 29 January 2025 and a government response has been published. Completing it is not certification.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22A: Automated processing and significant decisions
items.quote: Ch. 3 Section 4A substituted for Art. 22 (19.6.2025 for specified purposes, 5.2.2026 in so far as not already in force)
items.why: Source of the date in the brief. The UK's rules on automated decisions were replaced by Articles 22A to 22D, fully in force on 5 February 2026 (Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80(1); S.I. 2026/82). Any AI policy that still describes the old Article 22 is out of date, which is the practical test of currency the brief suggests.

items.title: AI Adoption Research
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (IFF Research and Technopolis Group)
items.locator: Chapter 6 (Perceptions of trust and safety in AI), "Using AI responsibly"
items.quote: Very few businesses said they had any internal guidelines or specific policies around using AI responsibly or ethically.
items.why: The best UK evidence found on how common AI policies are in business. From 100 follow-up interviews to a survey of 3,500 businesses carried out February to May 2025; larger businesses were more likely to have policies. Qualitative: no percentage is given, so the brief does not state one. The page shows only an update date (13 February 2026).

items.title: The Wates Corporate Governance Principles for Large Private Companies
items.locator: Principle Three (Director responsibilities), guidance on accountability, p.15
items.quote: A company should set out policies and practices that govern the internal affairs of the company.
items.why: The equivalent expectation for large private companies. The chair and company secretary should periodically review governance processes to confirm they remain fit for purpose. No mention of AI.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.quote: Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed, and documented.
items.why: International comparator for what a policy set should cover: GOVERN 1 asks for policies, processes, procedures and practices across the organisation that are 'in place, transparent, and implemented effectively'. Voluntary United States framework.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 113: Entry into force and application
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Art. 113, as amended (passages marked AMENDED and NEW)
items.why: Read to test the existing briefing's claim about EU duties 'from August 2026'. The general application date stands, but the 2026 amendments moved the high-risk chapters to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028, and Article 111 gives existing generative systems until 2 December 2026 to meet Article 50(2). The Commission's own copy, based on the consolidated text of 27 July 2026. The brief states no EU date; this entry supports the point that policies need a review trigger.

items.title: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank QPSC [2025] EWHC 1383 (Admin)
items.publisher: High Court of Justice, King's Bench Division, Divisional Court (The National Archives, Find Case Law)
items.quote: measures must now be taken by those within the legal profession with individual leadership responsibilities (such as heads of chambers and managing partners)
items.why: A Divisional Court judgment, after lawyers put fictitious AI-generated citations before the court, saying that those who lead legal practices must take practical and effective measures so that everyone understands their duties when using AI, and that courts will ask whether they did. The clearest UK judicial statement that rules on AI use are a leadership responsibility. Addressed to the legal profession in England and Wales; it does not prescribe a written policy by name.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 17: Quality management system
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: That system shall be documented in a systematic and orderly manner in the form of written policies, procedures and instructions
items.why: The binding EU rule that comes closest to requiring an AI policy set: providers of high-risk systems must document their quality management system as written policies, procedures and instructions, including an accountability framework. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text (stated as at 27 July 2026), not the Official Journal. Applies to providers of high-risk systems only, so it reaches UK firms only where they place such systems on the EU market; no application date is given here.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, Accountability toolkit: Policies and procedures
items.locator: Second control measure (review and approval process), list 'Ways to meet our expectations'; first control measure, 'Options to consider'
items.quote: Update policies and procedures without undue delay when they require changes, eg because of operational change, court or regulatory decisions or changes in regulatory guidance.
items.why: What the regulator's auditors test in a policy set: endorsed at the highest level of management, approved by a senior person, reviewed on documented dates, updated on legal or operational change, and backed by a mechanism to show staff have read it. It maps closely onto the levels of this criterion. Carries the 'under review' banner following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; the page shows no publication date, so the year is the year read. Data protection only, not AI governance in general.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, NIST AI 600-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Suggested action GV-1.4-002 (under GOVERN 1.4), printed p.15 (PDF p.19); see also GV-3.2-003 and GV-6.1-010
items.quote: Establish transparent acceptable use policies for GAI that address illegal use or applications of GAI.
items.why: A free standard, dated 2024, that turns the framework's general policy outcome into specific actions on acceptable-use policies for generative AI, including extending them to contractors and third-party tools. Voluntary, US, and limited to generative AI.

items.title: Principles alone cannot guarantee ethical AI
items.publisher: Brent Mittelstadt (arXiv; published in Nature Machine Intelligence)
items.quote: (3) proven methods to translate principles into practice, and (4) robust legal and professional accountability mechanisms
items.why: Peer-reviewed argument that statements of principle do little by themselves because AI development lacks tested ways to turn them into practice and lacks accountability mechanisms. The case for policies that carry owners, procedures and monitoring. Author's arXiv copy (version 2, February 2020) of the article in Nature Machine Intelligence 1, 501-507; the journal copy was not read. Conceptual, not empirical.

items.title: The Ethics of AI Ethics: An Evaluation of Guidelines
items.publisher: Thilo Hagendorff (arXiv; published in Minds and Machines)
items.quote: effectiveness of guidelines or ethical codes is almost zero and that they do not change the behavior of professionals from the tech community
items.why: Review of 21 major AI ethics guidelines (the count in this version) which reports a controlled study (McNamara and others, 2018; 63 students and 105 professional developers) finding that showing people a code of ethics made no significant difference to their decisions. Evidence that an unread or unenforced policy changes nothing, which is why adherence has to be measured. Author's arXiv copy (version 2) of the article in Minds and Machines (2020); the journal copy could not be read. The study it reports is a single vignette experiment on software engineers, cited here second-hand.
